# Information Subsectors Lead US Wage Growth, With Broadcasting Wages Up Nearly 17%


Written by


[Maggie Gunara](https://www.lendingtree.com/writer/maggie-gunara/)


Edited by


[Becca Stanek](https://www.lendingtree.com/writer/becca-stanek/)


Published Oct 26, 2026


Content was accurate at the time of publication.


We are committed to providing accurate content that helps you make informed money decisions. Our partners have not commissioned or endorsed this content. Read oureditorial guidelines here .


Pay is climbing across the private sector, but nowhere faster than in the information sector. Data shows average weekly wages in this sector rose 9.4% between 2024 and 2025 — and half of the 10 subsectors with the biggest pay gains were in the information sector.


Here’s a closer look.


Key findings


- **The information sector dominated wage growth.** Average weekly wages across private-sector industries increased 4.2% between 2024 and 2025, and five of the 10 subsectors with the fastest wage growth were in the information sector. Broadcasting and content providers led all subsectors, with average weekly wages increasing 16.8%, or $788.
- **Healthcare drove private-industry employment growth.** Annual average employment in the healthcare and social assistance sector increased 3.4% between 2024 and 2025 — far faster than the 0.4% increase across private-sector industries.
- **By subsector, social assistance led employment growth.** Annual average employment in social assistance increased by 300,984 workers, or 6.4%, between 2024 and 2025. The next largest employment gains also came from the healthcare and social assistance sector: ambulatory healthcare services (241,080), hospitals (111,863) and nursing and residential care facilities (109,551).
- **Outside healthcare, employment gains were much smaller.** The remaining subsectors in the top 10 accounted for just 25.6% of the roughly 1.03 million jobs added across the 10 fastest-growing subsectors. Among subsectors outside of the healthcare space, amusement, gambling and recreation added 55,170 jobs, followed by specialty trade contractors (53,710) and couriers and messengers (50,670).


## Information sector posts steepest wage gain


Between 2024 and 2025, average weekly wages rose 4.2% (or $62) across private-sector industries. Of the subsectors, broadcasting and content providers had the single largest pay increase, climbing 16.8% — a jump of $788 weekly.


Matt Schulz, LendingTree chief consumer finance analyst and author of “Ask Questions, Save Money, Make More: How to Take Control of Your Financial Life,” says that strong wage growth reflects serious demand for talent in those fields. This level of demand creates a real problem for smaller businesses.


“Trying to win a salary bidding war against a large information company may be a losing proposition, simply because that big firm has so many more resources,” he says. “That means that[small businesses](https://www.lendingtree.com/business/small/) may have to emphasize different things, such as flexibility or room for advancement, to get an edge. Of course, salary is a huge factor in determining where people want to work, but it isn’t the only one.”


Web search portals, libraries, archives and other information services was next, with an 11.0% increase, or $638. That was followed by publishing, where average weekly wages rose 9.9%, or $355. In total, five of the 10 subsectors with the fastest wage growth were in the information sector.


On the other hand, just one industry saw a decrease in weekly wages: the motion picture and sound recording industry. The industry posted a 2.0% (or $36) decrease in weekly wages from 2024 to 2025.

## Healthcare and social assistance outpaces other private-sector hiring


While the information sector is winning on pay, healthcare and social assistance is where the jobs are. Employment in this sector grew 3.4% between 2024 and 2025 — nearly nine times the 0.4% increase across private-sector industries.


Schulz believes that’s further proof that not every corner of the economy is booming.


“No one should be surprised that healthcare and social assistance is growing rapidly, especially as the nation’s population ages,” he says. “We also shouldn’t be surprised that the industry is appealing to lots of workers. While demand for other goods and services can have its peaks and valleys, demand for healthcare is persistent, which means that there will likely always be a need for workers in that field. That kind of predictability and security is a big deal. It also means that small businesses in other sectors may have to compete with the lure of the healthcare space to attract and keep employees.”


Following that, the arts, entertainment and recreation sector grew 2.4%, and utilities grew 2.2%. Meanwhile, nine of the 20 sectors analyzed saw a decrease in employment between 2024 and 2025. Mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction saw the largest decline (2.6%), followed by information (1.9%) and agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting (1.9%).

## Social assistance is the single fastest-growing subsector


Within healthcare and social assistance, social assistance itself is the standout: Employment there grew by 300,984 workers between 2024 and 2025 — a 6.4% increase. That marks the fastest employment growth of any qualifying subsector, and it’s more than any other subsector added in raw job numbers.


Schulz says there are a few reasons why this may be the case. “Our population is aging, with most boomers now well past retirement age,” he says. “That creates a massive strain on our healthcare system, but it creates real opportunity for small businesses. The healthcare space needs help with staffing,[payroll](https://www.lendingtree.com/business/payroll-financing/) , cybersecurity, cleaning and countless other services that small businesses may be better fit to provide than bigger companies. It’s up to companies to offer solutions for these needs and grow from there.”

## Job growth outside healthcare is comparatively modest


Strip healthcare out of the picture, and hiring in the remaining top subsectors looks a lot lower. Nonhealthcare subsectors in the top 10 accounted for just 25.6% of the roughly 1.03 million jobs added across the 10 fastest-growing subsectors (by number).


The largest of these outside healthcare were amusement, gambling and recreation (55,170), specialty trade contractors (53,710), and couriers and messengers (50,670).


Notably, only six qualifying subsectors outperformed the private-industry average in both employment and wage growth. They included: electrical equipment, appliance and component manufacturing; utilities; securities, commodity contracts and other financial investments; specialty trade contractors; animal production and aquaculture; and construction of buildings.


## Competing for talent without breaking the budget: Top expert tips


Small businesses may not always be able to outbid larger employers on pay, but compensation is only one part of what keeps good employees around. For small businesses in the most competitive industries, we offer the following advice:


- **Compete on more than pay.** “Don’t assume that competing for workers always means writing the biggest paycheck,” Schulz says. “Ask your best employees what keeps them around. Flexible schedules, opportunities to advance and feeling heard can make a meaningful difference.”
- **Invest in the employees you have.** “Turnover is expensive and disruptive, so retaining strong employees can pay off,” he says. “A well-timed raise or bonus may cost less than replacing a valued team member and training someone new.”
- **Look for other ways to strengthen your business.** Regularly reviewing staffing, benefits and[operating expenses](https://www.lendingtree.com/business/working-capital/) can help you find a balance between staying competitive and protecting your margins.


## Methodology


LendingTree analyzed annual average employment and average weekly wage data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) for U.S. private-sector industries, retrieved on Aug. 4, 2026.


Employment and wage growth were calculated by comparing 2024 and 2025 annual averages for private-sector three-digit and two-digit NAICS industries. The analysis was limited to sectors with at least 100,000 annual average employees in 2025.


Industries were ranked based on three criteria:


- Percentage growth in annual average employment
- The number of jobs added
- Percentage growth in average weekly wages

**Home Equity Loans and Home Equity Lines of Credit** are both secured by your home and generally require available equity in the property. If you become delinquent on your mortgage or home equity payments, you could lose your home through foreclosure. Before selecting either product, carefully consider your ability to repay the additional debt and review the interest rates, points, fees, repayment terms, and other conditions associated with the loan. Qualification depends on lender underwriting criteria, available home equity, and your ability to repay, and lenders may review factors such as your credit score, credit history, employment history, debt, income, and overall financial profile. Some lenders may also require that you maintain an account with them or meet minimum equity requirements. Generally, home equity loans are not available for homes currently listed for sale. Homes previously listed for sale may be required to remain off the market for at least 90 days prior to applying for a home equity loan or HELOC. Consumers should consult with a financial advisor or other professional before making financial decisions.


**Home Equity Loans** generally provide borrowers with a lump-sum loan amount secured by the equity in their home and typically feature a fixed interest rate and consistent monthly payments over the repayment term. Interest paid on a Home Equity Loan may be tax deductible; however, consumers should consult with a financial advisor or tax professional regarding their individual circumstances. Consumers should also ask lenders about any applicable prepayment penalties.


**Home Equity Lines of Credit (HELOC)** are revolving lines of credit secured by the equity in your home that allow borrowers to access funds during a defined draw period, such as 10 years. During the draw period, borrowers may draw funds as needed, repay amounts owed, and draw additional funds again, similar to the use of a credit card. HELOCs may be a suitable option for borrowers who do not need all available funds at one time. HELOCs generally have variable interest rates tied to a predefined index, such as the U.S. Prime Rate, which means monthly payment amounts may fluctuate over time. Repayment terms vary by lender and may include both a draw period and a repayment period, such as a 30-year term that includes a 10-year draw period. For more information, see[http://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/201204_CFPB_HELOC-brochure.pdf](http://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/201204_CFPB_HELOC-brochure.pdf) .
